commentary.bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether documenting provenance, design, validation, and limitations, or publishing according to reporting guidelines, improves reproduction, appraisal, or patient outcomes. Eight hazard studies show that reporting gaps are common, including FDA device summaries that omitted demographic information for 660 of 691 (95.5%) cleared AI/ML devices.

perspectives.view: No included study tests the practice, so certainty is rated as no direct evidence. The eight hazard studies use cross-sectional, descriptive, replay, or benchmark designs at levels 3 to 5. They consistently document reporting gaps. They cannot show that documentation or guideline adherence closes those gaps or changes how reviewers appraise a model.

In one Netherlands ECG study, the Georgia dataset lacked formal procedural documentation and showed weaker label consistency than the documented PTB-XL and Chapman-Shaoxing datasets. Sepsis-3 labels with identical names also differed across studies. These findings suggest undocumented choices may conceal label errors that carry into deployed models. Neither study tested documentation as a remedy.

Three published CNN studies omitted image pre-processing steps and random seeds. An external knee radiograph dataset lacked acquisition protocols, equipment, quality control, and label generation details, and one radiomics study had incomplete feature-level provenance. These gaps may prevent local teams from reproducing a model before implementation. No study measured the staff time or fidelity of producing such documentation.

Among 691 FDA-cleared AI/ML devices, 660 (95.5%) public summaries did not report demographic information. Without these data, a safety-net or Medicaid-serving system cannot judge whether its patients resemble the development population. None of the hazard studies reports whether its data included patients with limited English proficiency or low literacy.

FDA draft lifecycle guidance asks developers to report when data were acquired. In one review, public device summaries omitted study design for 323 (46.7%) and training sample size for 368 (53.3%) of 691 devices. This suggests public summaries often fall short of what guidance requests. No study tested whether regulatory requirements or enforcement change reporting completeness.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares models or evaluations documented according to TRIPOD-AI, STARD, or datasheet standards with models and evaluations that were not. Useful outcomes would include successful external replication, the accuracy of appraisal by health system reviewers, detection of residual risk before deployment, and patient harm. Studies should also measure the cost and staff time needed to produce reproducible documentation.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The hazard studies drew on U.S. device summaries and on datasets from the Netherlands, China, and Thailand, and none reported these population characteristics. Because demographic information was absent from 95.5% of FDA summaries, systems serving these groups may lack the information needed to judge whether a model applies to their patients.
